They also saw a way to equip independent restaurants to compete with larger chains: delivery could reduce the importance of prime real-estate locations, letting restaurants with good food reach customers from less-prime locations and potentially help local economies.

sections.heading: Keep exploring and test assumptions
sections.content: Droege’s approach was to keep a “very, very wide aperture” on ideas and keep digging into options that initially seemed bad, to find out whether that judgment was right. As one test, Uber put 10 convenience trucks with 250 product SKUs on the road in Washington, DC, but got almost no orders. He said the team had not understood what drew customers to convenience stores—for example, cigarettes, beer, and Slurpees—and admitted they were clueless about retail.

sections.heading: Compare the experiments with food delivery
sections.content: Uber also tried generalized point-to-point delivery, which Droege said flopped: in 2014 consumers did not seem to need it, and businesses did not yet have that need either. Grocery was another possibility, but he said the pick-and-pack unit economics were intimidating. After trying 15 versions of these ideas, the team focused on food delivery because it was “popping off on all signals,” people seemed to want it, and they believed they could make the unit economics work.

sections.heading: Why food delivery won
sections.content: Droege saw food delivery as a way to equip independent restaurants to compete with larger chains. Delivery could remove prime real estate as a requirement: a restaurant in a non-prime location could compete if it had prime food. He also viewed the opportunity as a way to help local economies. This is the sequence implied by his account: keep exploring, learn from failed tests, then choose the idea with stronger demand, workable economics, and a compelling local-business opportunity.
